reference.source: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
clinicalPearls: A flexion-distraction injury of the spine, classically at the thoracolumbar junction, from a lap belt in rapid deceleration
The classic bony Chance fracture runs horizontally, splitting the posterior elements, pedicles and vertebral body
The fulcrum lies anterior to the spine, so the posterior and middle columns fail under tension while the anterior column acts as a hinge
There is a strong association with intra-abdominal injuries (hollow viscus, mesenteric and pancreatic), heralded by the seatbelt sign bruise across the abdomen
Purely osseous injuries through cancellous bone may heal in a hyperextension brace, whereas ligamentous variants and those with neurological deficit or instability require surgical fixation
Look specifically for abdominal wall ecchymosis and screen for visceral injury
Increased interspinous distance on imaging is a clue to the distraction component
reference.pathophysiology: A flexion-distraction force with its fulcrum anterior to the spine, as when a lap belt restrains the pelvis during sudden deceleration, places the posterior and middle spinal columns under tension. Failure propagates horizontally, either through bone in the classic Chance fracture, through the disc and ligaments in a purely soft-tissue variant, or through a combination of both. The same abrupt flexion compresses the abdominal viscera against the spine, explaining the frequent association with hollow viscus and mesenteric injuries. Whether the injury is stable depends on the integrity of the posterior ligamentous complex.
additionalDifferentials: Fracture in ankylosing spondylitis or diffuse skeletal hyperostosis
additionalInvestigations: Anteroposterior and lateral spinal radiographs, noting increased interspinous distance
CT to define the bony injury and involvement of the spinal columns
MRI to assess the posterior ligamentous complex and the spinal cord or soft tissues
CT of the abdomen and pelvis to screen for associated visceral injuries
redFlags: Associated intra-abdominal or visceral injury signalled by a seatbelt sign
A ligamentous (unstable) variant of the injury
reference.prognosis: Purely osseous injuries through cancellous bone generally heal well with bracing, whereas ligamentous variants are unstable and require fixation; associated abdominal injuries may dominate the early clinical course.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise a ligamentous variant by relying on CT without MRI
Underestimating the instability of the injury
Overlooking the fracture on inadequate imaging
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Manage stable, purely osseous Chance fractures with immobilisation in a hyperextension thoracolumbosacral orthosis and serial radiographic follow-up
Treat ligamentous or unstable variants, and those with neurological deficit, with posterior instrumented fixation and fusion
Screen actively for associated intra-abdominal injury involving hollow viscus, mesentery and pancreas, prompted by a seatbelt-sign bruise, with CT imaging and early surgical involvement
Perform and document a full neurological examination and maintain spinal precautions and log-rolling until stability is established
Provide analgesia, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis and early mobilisation once the injury is stabilised
Refer to orthopaedic or spinal trauma services, with trauma-team and general-surgical input for concomitant visceral injury
Arrange rehabilitation and monitor brace-treated fractures for loss of reduction or progressive deformity
